```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(descriptr)
library(dplyr)
```

## Introduction

In this document, we will introduce you to functions for exploring and 
visualizing categorical data.

## Data

The `wholesale_customers` data set records annual spending by 440 wholesale
customers on six product categories, along with the sales channel and region of
each customer. Both `channel` and `region` are factors.

```{r egdata}
str(wholesale_customers)
```

## Cross Tabulation

The `ds_cross_table()` function creates two way tables of categorical variables. 
The table below crosses the customer channel with the region. Of the 298
hotel/restaurant/cafe customers, 211 (70.81%) are in the other region, as are
105 of the 142 retail customers (73.94%).

```{r cross}
ds_cross_table(wholesale_customers, channel, region)
```

If you want the above result as a tibble, use `ds_twoway_table()`.

```{r cross_tibble}
ds_twoway_table(wholesale_customers, channel, region)
```

A `plot()` method has been defined which will generate:

### Grouped Bar Plots

```{r cross_group, fig.width=7, fig.height=7, fig.align='centre'}
k <- ds_cross_table(wholesale_customers, channel, region)
plot(k)
```

### Stacked Bar Plots

```{r cross_stack, fig.width=7, fig.height=7, fig.align='centre'}
k <- ds_cross_table(wholesale_customers, channel, region)
plot(k, stacked = TRUE)
```

### Proportional Bar Plots

```{r cross_prop, fig.width=7, fig.height=7, fig.align='centre'}
k <- ds_cross_table(wholesale_customers, channel, region)
plot(k, proportional = TRUE)
```

## Frequency Table 

The `ds_freq_table()` function creates frequency tables. Of the 440 customers,
298 (67.73%) are in the hotel/restaurant/cafe channel and 142 (32.27%) are in
retail.

```{r ftable}
ds_freq_table(wholesale_customers, channel)
```

A `plot()` method has been defined which will create a bar plot.

```{r ftable_bar, fig.width=7, fig.height=7, fig.align='centre'}
k <- ds_freq_table(wholesale_customers, channel)
plot(k)
```

## Multiple One Way Tables

The `ds_auto_freq_table()` function creates multiple one way tables by creating a 
frequency table for each categorical variable in a data set. You can also 
specify a subset of variables if you do not want all the variables in the data 
set to be used. The data set has two categorical variables, so one table is
created for each. Most customers (316, 71.82%) are in the other region; 77
(17.50%) are in Lisbon and 47 (10.68%) are in Porto.

```{r oway}
ds_auto_freq_table(wholesale_customers)
```

## Multiple Two Way Tables

The `ds_auto_cross_table()` function creates multiple two way tables by creating a 
cross table for each unique pair of categorical variables in a data set. You 
can also specify a subset of variables if you do not want all the variables in 
the data set to be used. Since `channel` and `region` are the only categorical
variables, we first derive a third one: total annual spend across the six
categories, split at its tertiles into `low`, `medium` and `high` spending
bands. That gives 147, 146 and 147 customers in the three bands. Three tables
are then created: channel by region, channel by spend band and region by spend
band.

```{r tway}
customers <- wholesale_customers %>%
  mutate(
    total_spend = fresh + milk + grocery + frozen + detergents_paper + delicassen,
    spend_band  = cut(
      total_spend,
      breaks = quantile(total_spend, c(0, 1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1)),
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      labels = c("low", "medium", "high")
    )
  )

ds_auto_cross_table(customers)
```

The spend band separates the channels: 85 of the 142 retail customers (59.86%)
are in the high band, against 62 of the 298 hotel/restaurant/cafe customers
(20.81%). Region, by contrast, is not associated with spending: the other
region splits almost evenly across the bands (108 low, 99 medium, 109 high).
